source.title: QM2017: Status and Key open Questions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Physics

accepted.question_text: What microscopic mechanisms generate approximately thermal or statistical hadron-species particle ratios across high-energy reactions from electron-positron collisions through proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions to central nucleus-nucleus collisions, when statistical models fit many ratios with very few parameters but existing experiments do not conclusively show whether the system evolves into equilibrium through reactions and detailed balance or is born into an equilibrium-like state dominated by phase space?

evidence.quote: By far the most economic and successful model of particle production (hadronisation) in high energy collisions is the thermal or statistical model, which describes dozens of particle ratios in different high energy reactions (from e+e− over pp/pA to AA) with very few free parameters; in fact a single one - the chemical freeze-out temperature Tchem - in nuclear collisions at LHC.

The underlying idea of statistical equilibrium distributions is simple and intuitive, but despite decades of success and a number of plausible ideas, there is not a single experimental result which would tell us conclusively how or why it works as well as it does.
What mechanisms generate the statistical particle ratios, from e+e− to central AA, or produce (the mirage of?) a strongly interacting liquid in tiny systems containing a mere handful of particles?

accepted.question_text: Can out-of-equilibrium remnants and particle-specific freeze-out hierarchies be identified and measured well enough to reconstruct the dynamics of hadronisation, including how different reaction channels and hadronic cross sections cause different particle species to freeze out at different times and temperatures?

evidence.quote: If equilibrium is the problem, hiding dynamics, looking for out-of-equilibrium remnants may be the solution to uncover dynamics.

Therefore, given the large variety of reaction channels and hadronic cross sections, it is not a question of if different particles will freeze-out at different times and temperatures, but only a question of how big the effect is in each individual case.
Identifying such a freeze-out hierarchy in certain particle ratios could make, not break, the case for hadro-chemistry!

accepted.question_text: How should thermal or statistical descriptions of hadronisation explain the observed dependence of particle ratios on system size and particle density from minimum-bias proton-proton events to central nucleus-nucleus collisions, including the failure of an event-by-event strangeness-canonical picture for the φ/π ratio and the absence of an analogous proton suppression at LHC baryochemical potential μB = 0?

evidence.quote: One way of looking for "dynamics at work" are the recent studies of size and density (dN/dy) dependence of particle ratios in pp and pA, some of them to be shown at this conference.

Without any initial or final state interactions (i.e. additional dynamics), there seems no obvious mechanism how the "born into phase space" idea can describe the significant change of particles ratios from MinBias pp to central AA.

The observed pattern is intriguing and non-trivial also in the context of the statistical model, as the strangeness canonical version (exact Event-by-Event (EbE) strangeness conservation) fails the crucial φ/π test.

In addition, at LHC (μB=0), baryon conservation should be as relevant as strangeness conservation. However, no suppression is seen for protons while one could naively expect the effect to be roughly similar to the one measured for kaons or lambdas (somebody should do the actual calculation!).

accepted.question_text: What mechanism explains the surprisingly low proton-to-pion ratio at the LHC despite fits with a reduced chemical freeze-out temperature, and can baryon final-state annihilation or late baryon freeze-out be distinguished from other explanations without creating tension with hyperon abundances and resonance-ratio constraints?

evidence.quote: Another hint of non-equilibrium may be the surprisingly low p/π-ratio at LHC; despite pulling down by almost 10 MeV the chemical freeze-out temperature compared to pre-LHC fits - which leads to a slight tension with some Hyperon abundances which seem to prefer the original Tchem - the p/π-ratio remains well below most predictions.
Amongst a number of possible explanations, baryon final state annihilation (i.e. late baryon freeze-out) is a leading but not the only contender.

Resonance ratios are therefore a sensitive measure of the final state interaction taking place after hadronisation; they are well described by transport codes (EPOS, URQMD) and consequently strongly disfavour models with a single (Tchem=Tkin) chemical and kinetic freeze-out.

accepted.question_text: Are light antinuclei such as deuterium, tritium, helium-3, hypertriton, and helium-4 produced thermally at the phase boundary or by nucleon coalescence near kinetic freeze-out, and how can these lightly bound nuclei survive the later kinetic scattering phase despite MeV-scale binding energies and very large inelastic breakup cross sections?

evidence.quote: A puzzle, around since more than 30 years, has returned with a vengeance at the colliders: the production of light (anti)nuclei (d, t, 3He, 3ΛH, 4He).

Two models compete to explain their yields and momentum distributions: Thermal/statistical production, like any other hadron, right at the phase boundary followed by kinetic expansion, or coalescence of nucleons into nuclei at around kinetic freeze-out.

The puzzle however is how these lightly bound nuclei survive the kinetic scattering phase intact until kinetic freeze-out, given the small energy threshold (typical binding energy is MeV or less) and the huge cross sections (the inelastic cross section for pion deuteron break-up exceeds 100mb and is actually larger than the elastic cross section!).

For the time being, nucleosynthesis remains as puzzling as ever, but detailed transport calculations (including inelastic reactions with realistic break-up cross sections) are urgently needed to make the discussion quantitative.

accepted.question_text: Does the initial temperature inferred from excess direct photons in heavy-ion collisions increase from RHIC to LHC energies, and can higher-precision photon measurements plus calculations with medium-modified rates and state-of-the-art space-time evolution establish that trend?

evidence.quote: The inverse slopes of the direct photon excess (≈200 MeV at RHIC and ≈300 MeV at LHC) can be related to a temperature only in a model dependent way (because of space-time averaging and flow blue shift), but indicate initial temperatures of order T0 ≈300 - 500 MeV, far above Tc.

A number of key issues remain to be addressed for direct photons: on the experimental side primarily reducing errors (stat+syst) to confirm that T0 indeed increases with energy between RHIC and LHC, as the current evidence is only marginally significant; on the theory side more detailed calculations including e.g. medium effects on rates and state-of-the-art space-time evolution.

accepted.question_text: Why is the elliptic flow v2 of direct photons in heavy-ion collisions as large as the charged-particle v2 within sizeable experimental errors, and what theoretical ingredients are needed for hydrodynamic or radiation-rate models to reproduce it quantitatively?

evidence.quote: Describing the direct photon v2, which is within (sizeable!) errors as large as the v2 of charged particles, remains a major challenge; even unorthodox choices of model parameters (eg for the transition temperature Tc) often lead to only a moderate agreement between data and theory.

Amongst the many open questions and active areas of current research are: the elliptic flow of photons and heavy flavours, both measured to be typically larger than calculated by hydro; collectivity in small systems (discussed later); the hydro decoupling regime at intermediate pT of between a few and 10 GeV.

accepted.question_text: What is the precise theoretical connection between the observed broadening or melting of the ρ meson in hot hadronic matter and chiral symmetry restoration in the quark-gluon plasma, and can missing LHC, intermediate-mass, and small-system dilepton data determine whether collective features in small systems accompany hot-matter formation?

evidence.quote: The connection between the observed broadening of the ρ in hot hadronic matter and chiral symmetry restoration in the QGP is however still more of a conjecture than a solid theoretical derivation.

On the experimental side, precision results from LHC are still missing, and may have to wait a few years for detector upgrades. Likewise needed is better data on the intermediate mass region (thermal radiation, charm) from both RHIC and LHC, and ideally even in pp/pA to see if the collective features observed in small systems go hand in hand with "hot matter".

accepted.question_text: Can J/ψ regeneration during hadronisation be established quantitatively as evidence for deconfinement and colour conductivity by measuring the total charm cross section, finding a second unambiguous heavy-quark recombination channel such as Bc production, and excluding final-state hadronic D + D recombination into J/ψ + X?

evidence.quote: Redemption, so it is hoped, may have finally arrived in the form of an increased J/ψ RAA at LHC, whose pT and centrality dependence neatly shows the predicted hallmarks of J/ψ regeneration during hadronisation.

Deconfinement implies colour conductivity, i.e. coloured partons can roam freely over distances much larger than the deconfinement scale. Such long distance travel is exactly what is needed in the regeneration model to explain how charm quarks produced in independent initial hard parton collisions can find each other at later times to recombine into a J/ψ during hadronisation.

However, given the charming history, some extra care and additional checks may be in order before declaring victory: to be quantitative, regeneration calculations need as input the total charm cross section (missing so far); a second unambiguous example for heavy quark recombination would be very helpful (eg Bc); the spectre of final state recombination at the hadron (D + D → J/ψ + X) rather than parton level has to be very convincingly excluded.

accepted.question_text: Can a complete and coherent theory describe quarkonium suppression and regeneration for both J/ψ and Υ families across SPS, RHIC, and LHC energies, including whether sequential Υ melting changes with temperature between RHIC and LHC once lattice-QCD spectral functions, cold nuclear matter effects, energy loss, co-movers, hydrodynamic evolution, heavy-quark diffusion, and feed-down are all included?

evidence.quote: The original deconfinement signal, sequential quarkonia suppression (RAAΥ(1)> Υ(2)> Υ(3)), has been observed at LHC for the Υ family.

Together with RHIC data (and smaller error bars), we may be able to see experimentally the effect of raising the temperature, if the melting pattern of different Υ states would change between the two energies. However, so far it seems that the RAA of Υ is very much comparable at RHIC and LHC (Déjà vu?).

Although the theory description of heavy quark suppression has advanced significantly, a complete and fully coherent description of all quarkonium data (J/ψ and Υ families) at SPS/RHIC/LHC needs significant further work (e.g. to include all of lQCD spectral functions, CNM effects like PDFs, energy loss, co-movers, hydro evolution, heavy quark diffusion, feed-down, ..).

accepted.question_text: Why do measured elliptic-flow signals of photons and heavy flavours in heavy-ion collisions tend to be larger than hydrodynamic calculations predict, and what does resolving this discrepancy imply for the space-time evolution and transport properties of the strongly coupled quark-gluon plasma?

evidence.quote: Amongst the many open questions and active areas of current research are: the elliptic flow of photons and heavy flavours, both measured to be typically larger than calculated by hydro; collectivity in small systems (discussed later); the hydro decoupling regime at intermediate pT of between a few and 10 GeV.

The increasing accuracy, together with novel observables and analysis methods like Bayesian multi-parameter fits, have led to a significant improvement in both constraining the sQGP (e.g. shear and bulk viscosity), as well as the detailed spatial structure of the initial state.

accepted.question_text: How does hydrodynamic behavior decouple from hadron production at intermediate transverse momentum between a few and 10 GeV, where hadrons are increasingly poorly described by hydrodynamics but not yet fully described by perturbative-QCD jets, and what physical interpretation, if any, remains for constituent-quark scaling in that transition region?
accepted.context_brief: Intermediate-pT hydro decoupling and quark scaling

evidence.quote: Amongst the many open questions and active areas of current research are: the elliptic flow of photons and heavy flavours, both measured to be typically larger than calculated by hydro; collectivity in small systems (discussed later); the hydro decoupling regime at intermediate pT of between a few and 10 GeV, where hadrons are increasingly less well described by hydro but not yet fully by pQCD and jets.
Quark scaling (NCQ) remains an intriguing regularity in the data, but unlike hydro has unfortunately not progressed much from the initial back-of-the envelope scaling relations.

accepted.question_text: In ultra-central heavy-ion collisions with centrality below 1%, why are the second- and third-harmonic flow coefficients v2 and v3 observed to be about the same even though fluctuation-dominated initial eccentricities are expected to satisfy ε2 ≈ ε3 and positive shear viscosity should damp v3 more strongly than v2?

evidence.quote: And finally, one open problem remains unsolved since the first realisation that v2 and v3 are about the same in very central collisions (< 1% centrality): Despite several attempts, no model or parameter set has been able to reconcile these results with the expectation, i.e. ε2 ≈ ε3 when fluctuations dominate, and therefore v3 < v2 with viscous damping η/S > 0.
As both data and the predictions seem very solid, the solution may be relevant even if it is more likely to be a thorny problem rather than a crack in the heavy ion standard model.

accepted.question_text: Are the charge-specific multi-particle correlations observed in heavy-ion collisions genuine Chiral Magnetic signals from QCD chiral anomaly effects in strong magnetic fields, or are they backgrounds produced by local charge conservation modulated by elliptic flow, and can proposed parameter-isolating tests such as isobar-beam collisions deliver a decisive limit or answer?

evidence.quote: QCD chiral symmetry, and its violation by quantum effects ("chiral anomaly"), leads in the presence of strong external magnetic fields to a number of charge specific multi-particle correlations commonly referred to as "Chiral Magnetic".

Unfortunately, not all of the observed systematics (pT, √s, correlation with the EP, ..) follow precisely the prediction, and also making the strongly Lorentz contracted magnetic field decay slowly enough to have any measureable effect at all is nontrivial.

Therefore, the leading background explanation of local charge conservation modulated by elliptic flow remains a very strong contender, even if it has its own problems with some of the observed regularities.
Eventually a future test at RHIC with isobar beams (|B| not equal const, v2 = const) could set a decisive limit if the question has not been settled by then.

accepted.question_text: What response, if any, does a strongly coupled quark-gluon plasma produce after a jet deposits concentrated local energy, and can high-statistics measurements, especially γ-jet measurements and new detector data, identify medium responses such as a Mach cone or collective wake?

evidence.quote: Amongst the open questions is identifying the response, if any, of the medium to the concentrated local energy deposition (Mach Cone, collective wake,..).

Future high precision measurements with more statistics, in particular in the golden γ-jet channel, and new detectors (sPHENIX), are needed to confirm the ever so slight hint of a non-trivial temperature dependence of the stopping power (RHIC → LHC) and nail its parton type, parton energy, and path-length dependence.

accepted.question_text: What are the temperature, parton-type, parton-energy, and path-length dependences of the jet-quenching stopping power q-hat divided by T cubed, and why do spectral slopes, fragmentation functions, and energy-loss coefficients appear to cancel so that the nuclear-modification factor RAA has nearly invariant magnitude and shape across parton flavours and collision energies?

evidence.quote: The "stopping power of sQGP", q̂/T3, is now known to about 30% and the predicted mass dependence has been investigated with heavy flavour mesons.

Future high precision measurements with more statistics, in particular in the golden γ-jet channel, and new detectors (sPHENIX), are needed to confirm the ever so slight hint of a non-trivial temperature dependence of the stopping power (RHIC → LHC) and nail its parton type, parton energy, and path-length dependence.

And finally, somewhat unsettling remains, at least to this author, the miraculous cancellations required concurrently in spectral slopes, fragmentation functions, and energy loss coefficients, in order to explain the nearly invariant magnitude and shape of RAA for different parton flavours (g ≈ u/d/s ≈ c ≈ b ≈ J/ψ) and at different energies (0.2 ≈ 2.8 ≈ 5 TeV).

accepted.question_text: Are long-range near-side ridge correlations and collective multi-particle flow signals in high-multiplicity proton-proton, proton-nucleus, deuteron-nucleus, and helium-nucleus collisions generated primarily by initial-state Colour Glass Condensate quantum correlations or by final-state interactions that create hydrodynamic collective flow?
accepted.context_brief: Origin of collectivity in small systems

evidence.quote: Two serious contenders remain today, i) initial state quantum correlations as calculated by CGC and ii) final state interactions leading to collective flow described with hydrodynamics.

As of today, all results clearly and unambiguously point into the same direction: The correlations seen in small (pp/pA/dA/HeA) systems are truly collective (i.e. v{4} ≈ v{6} ≈ v{8}..) and bear all the hallmarks of hydrodynamic flow as previously seen only in nuclear collisions.

A crucial test, and a triumph for the hydro explanation, was the correlation measurement at RHIC using d and 3He projectiles to introduce particular initial state geometries. The 2nd and 3rd harmonic flow components were exactly as predicted by hydro codes, whereas the CGC model is still toiling to find a convincing explanation.

accepted.question_text: How can hydrodynamic behavior remain applicable in small and dilute collision systems, including proton-proton and proton-nucleus events, where the mean free path relative to system size and the number of collisions per particle appear to fall outside the usual hydrodynamic regime?

evidence.quote: Were it not for the difficulty to conceive of hydrodynamic behaviour not only in small and dense, but also in small and dilute systems, where hydro is thought to be well outside its range of applicability (mean free path/system size << 1 and #collisions/particle << 1, see however [40]), the well-motivated but increasingly Ptolemaic CGC explanation would have had to concede defeat a while ago, given the clear preponderance of evidence.

While hydrodynamic codes can and are being used in ever smaller systems, down to pp at LHC, and actually give very consistent and coherent results well in line with the data, the debate does (and should) continue until we do understand the causes and the actual dynamics behind what is yet another case for an unreasonably successful model (hydro in small dilute systems).
What is the underlying dynamics, which makes thermalisation (if really achieved?) seemingly so fast, including in small and possibly even in dilute systems?

accepted.question_text: Can microscopic transport models describe both large dense nucleus-nucleus systems and small dilute systems, as well as the transition between them, well enough to explain the actual dynamics behind collective correlations, particle spectra, and particle ratios?

evidence.quote: Insight into the dynamics should come from checking how well microscopic transport models describe both large/dense and small/dilute systems and the transition between them.

One of the widely used transport codes, AMPT, can reproduce surprisingly well most two- and multi-particle correlation measures for all pA and AA systems at both RHIC and LHC (it is less good in describing pT spectra and particle ratios).

accepted.question_text: Are pressure tomography from hydrodynamics and density tomography from AMPT-like transport two limits of the same collective physics, or are they distinct mechanisms with experimentally separable consequences such as directed photon flow or nonlinear mode mixing?
accepted.context_brief: AMPT density tomography versus hydrodynamic pressure tomography

evidence.quote: Dubbed "Escape Mechanism", but better qualified as "density tomography", the AMPT transport generates an image of the initial state density distribution with single parton scatterings, which obviously leads to a depletion of particles in the direction of increased matter density.

For the time being, it is unclear (to this author) if pressure tomography as implied by hydro and density tomography as implied by AMPT are two sides of the same coin (the high and low density limits, respectively), or are two different physics mechanism with different observable consequences (say in directed photon flow or non-liner mode mixing).
The former would make the question moot, the latter would open it to experimental examination.

accepted.question_text: Is the physics underlying soft collective signals and apparently hadronisation the same in all high-energy reactions, from electron-positron events through proton-proton and proton-nucleus reactions to central nucleus-nucleus collisions, perhaps as a generic property of strongly interacting many-body systems with two or more particles?

evidence.quote: We should examine a new paradigm, where the physics underlying soft 'collective' signals (including apparently hadronisation!) is the same in all high energy reactions, from e+e− to central AA.
This physics may be a generic property of all strongly interacting many-body systems (N ≥ 2?), even if it is obvious and dominant only in AA and barely discernible in pp.

accepted.question_text: Is there an identifiable onset of the strongly coupled quark-gluon plasma as a function of collision time, beam energy, volume, system size, or energy density, and how does collectivity and macroscopic behavior emerge as those conditions are varied?

evidence.quote: In the dash to new machines and higher energy, the question of the onset - exactly when (in time) and where (in energy or volume) we first produced the QGP - has been left behind, unanswered.

For the time being, there are many hints, but no conclusive picture. It may yet turn out that there is actually no clearly identifiable onset, that the transition is continuous and gradual in terms of volume (starting with pp) or energy density, and possibly even happens at different places for different observables.
Is there an onset of the sQGP, and how does collectivity and macroscopic behaviour emerge with system size and/or energy density?

accepted.question_text: Does the QCD phase diagram contain a critical point and a first-order phase transition at high baryon density, and can beam-energy scans and low-energy heavy-ion programs locate them through matter properties at large baryochemical potential?
accepted.context_brief: Critical point at high baryon density

evidence.quote: Besides the onset, the other landmark still missing in the phase diagram is the conjectured critical point, tentatively located at large baryon density and therefore at low beam energy.
Both questions, onset and critical point, are addressed with the past and future beam energy scans at RHIC and an energy-volume mapping ongoing at the SPS.
Is there a critical point and a first order phase transition at high baryon density?

accepted.question_text: What are the relevant microscopic degrees of freedom in the strongly interacting quark-gluon plasma if they are not quasi-free quarks and gluons, and how can precision measurements of macroscopic properties and transport coefficients identify them?

evidence.quote: We have measured with increasing precision its macroscopic properties and many transport coefficients (EOS, cS, η/S, ξ/S, D, q̂, ê); we have good evidence for deconfinement from J/ψ regeneration (colour conductivity) and sequential Υ suppression (resonance melting); we have some indirect evidence for chiral symmetry restoration (ρ melting, strangeness enhancement).
And we also learned that the d.o.f. of the Quark-Gluon Plasma are definitely not (quasi-free) quarks and gluons.
On a deeper level, much also remains to be discovered: Primarily, what are actually the relevant degrees of freedom?

accepted.question_text: What underlying dynamics makes thermalisation in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion and small-system collisions appear so fast, if thermalisation is really achieved, including in tiny or dilute systems where only a handful of particles may be present?

evidence.quote: What is the underlying dynamics, which makes thermalisation (if really achieved?) seemingly so fast, including in small and possibly even in dilute systems?
What mechanisms generate the statistical particle ratios, from e+e− to central AA, or produce (the mirage of?) a strongly interacting liquid in tiny systems containing a mere handful of particles?
